title: Common Questions on College Applications
checked: Research checked September 19, 2026. Scope: U.S. first-year undergraduate applications, with emphasis on essays and short answers.
overview: Overview and how to use this list

The recurring questions in the reviewed sources concern academic interests, personal background, challenges, community contribution, and fit with a college or program. These themes appear across the Common App, University of California, and individual college questions, although the wording and response formats differ (Common App, UC, Michigan, Yale).

This is a practical list of 30 questions to prepare for, not a statistically ranked national “top 30.” No nationwide question-frequency dataset was identified in the reviewed sources. The questions below are normalized paraphrases, not verbatim application text, and their order is an editorial preparation sequence rather than a measured frequency ranking.

Research covers the Common App and official admissions pages for UC, Yale, Michigan, MIT, and Tufts. Common App, Yale, and MIT explicitly identify 2026–27 questions; Tufts identifies the Class of 2031, while the reviewed UC and Michigan pages do not explicitly label an application cycle (Common App, Yale, MIT, Tufts, UC, Michigan).

The college-specific sample leans toward selective institutions and is not representative of every U.S. college. Schools may make the personal essay required or optional, and not all schools have writing supplements (Common App application guide).
coreIntro: These first twelve questions are useful starting points for an applicant’s preparation. The final column offers suggested brainstorming directions, not claims about an admissions scoring rubric.

core.question: What do you want to study, and why does it interest you?
core.examples: Yale asks applicants to identify academic areas and explain an exciting related topic; MIT asks what led to an interest in a field; UC asks about an inspiring academic subject (Yale, MIT, UC).
core.preparation: Identify how the interest started, how you pursued it, and what you want to explore next.

core.question: What background, identity, interest, or talent is essential to understanding you?
core.examples: Common App offers a background/identity/interest/talent prompt; Yale asks how a personal experience shaped the applicant and could enrich college (Common App, Yale).
core.preparation: Choose a concrete experience that reveals something not obvious from grades and activities.

core.question: Describe a challenge, setback, or failure. How did you respond, and what did you learn?
core.examples: Variations appear in Common App, UC, and MIT questions (Common App, UC, MIT).
core.preparation: Prepare the situation, your actions, the outcome, and an honest reflection.

core.question: How have you contributed to your community, and how will you contribute in college?
core.examples: UC asks about improving a school or community; Michigan asks how applicants will contribute to its leadership and citizenship goals; MIT connects future impact with personal and academic experiences (UC, Michigan, MIT).
core.preparation: Distinguish past contributions from future intentions, and make your individual role clear.

core.question: Why this college, school, or academic program?
core.examples: Michigan directly asks about the qualities of the specific undergraduate school and how its curriculum supports the applicant’s interests; Tufts asks the related but distinct question of how applicants learned about and engaged with Tufts (Michigan, Tufts).
core.preparation: Connect your interests to specific opportunities. Do not treat “why us?” and “how did you engage with us?” as interchangeable.

core.question: What idea or topic excites your curiosity?
core.examples: Common App asks about an absorbing topic; Yale asks about an exciting academic idea; MIT asks what topic the applicant could discuss for hours (Common App, Yale, MIT).
core.preparation: Explain what fascinates you and show how you explore it independently.

core.question: What experience or realization changed how you understand yourself or others?
core.examples: Common App asks about an accomplishment, event, or realization that sparked personal growth; Yale asks how personal experience shaped the applicant (Common App, Yale).
core.preparation: Describe a meaningful before-and-after change in your thinking or behavior.

core.question: Which activities, work, or responsibilities matter most to you?
core.examples: Common App collects activities, work, hobbies, community engagement, and responsibilities; MIT asks applicants to describe their four most meaningful activities (Common App guide, MIT).
core.preparation: Identify what you did, who benefited, and why the commitment matters.

core.question: Tell us about a time you led, influenced others, or helped a group succeed.
core.examples: UC has a direct leadership prompt; Michigan’s contribution essay centers on developing leaders and citizens (UC, Michigan).
core.preparation: Look for actions and effects, not just a title.

core.question: Describe a time you questioned an idea or engaged with someone who disagreed with you.
core.examples: Common App asks about questioning or challenging a belief; Yale asks about a meaningful discussion with someone holding an opposing view (Common App, Yale).
core.preparation: Separate the two versions: changing your own thinking versus engaging with another person.

core.question: What community do you belong to, and why is it meaningful?
core.examples: Yale asks directly about membership in a meaningful community; Common App’s background and identity prompt provides a possible route for a related story (Yale, Common App).
core.preparation: Explain your connection, your role, and how the community has shaped you.

core.question: What else should we know that is missing from your application?
core.examples: Yale has a short take on something not included elsewhere; MIT has an additional-information box; UC asks what else makes the applicant a strong candidate (Yale, MIT, UC).
core.preparation: Identify important missing context, but distinguish a personality question from a factual additional-information field.

additionalIntro: These questions broaden the preparation list, but several are specific to a platform or college. Their inclusion does not imply they appear on most applications.

additional.question: What is your greatest talent or skill, and how have you developed it?
additional.where: UC asks this directly; Common App includes talent in its background/identity prompt (UC, Common App).

additional.question: How do you express creativity or solve problems in an original way?
additional.where: UC explicitly asks about creativity, including artistic expression, original thinking, and problem-solving (UC).

additional.question: How have you used an educational opportunity or overcome an educational barrier?
additional.where: UC asks this directly; MIT separately asks about doing something unexpected in one’s educational journey (UC, MIT).

additional.question: What has someone done for you that inspired gratitude, and how did it affect you?
additional.where: This is one of the seven Common App personal-essay options (Common App).

additional.question: What do you do just for fun?
additional.where: MIT asks this as a short response (MIT).

additional.question: Who do you admire, and why?
additional.where: MIT asks applicants to identify someone they admire, whether personally known or admired from afar (MIT).

additional.question: Describe a favorite assignment, project, or creative work and explain your role or thinking.
additional.where: Tufts uses different versions for Arts and Sciences, Engineering, BFA, and combined-degree applicants (Tufts).

additional.question: What aspect of yourself do you hope to grow or develop during college?
additional.where: Yale includes this among its short takes for Common App and Coalition applicants (Yale).

routineIntro: Applications also collect factual information rather than narrative essays. The questions below paraphrase information categories in Common App’s first-year guide; exact fields and whether they are required vary by institution and applicant (Common App application guide).

routine.question: What are your high school grades?
routine.evidence: The Education section collects grades; some colleges also require a self-reported transcript (Common App guide).

routine.question: What courses are you taking now?
routine.evidence: Current courses are collected in the Education section (Common App guide).

routine.question: What academic honors or achievements have you earned?
routine.evidence: Applicants have an opportunity to report high school academic honors and achievements (Common App guide).

routine.question: What clubs, extracurricular activities, and hobbies do you participate in?
routine.evidence: These are examples of information for the Activities section (Common App guide).

routine.question: What paid work or other responsibilities do you have?
routine.evidence: Common App identifies work and responsibilities as relevant application information (Common App guide).

routine.question: What community engagement have you participated in?
routine.evidence: Community engagement is another Activities section example (Common App guide).

routine.question: What standardized tests have you taken, and what are your scores?
routine.evidence: Applicants may self-report test scores; testing policies differ by college (Common App guide).

routine.question: What are your parents’ or guardians’ occupations and employment status?
routine.evidence: Common App identifies these as Family section information (Common App guide).

routine.question: What education have your parents or guardians completed?
routine.evidence: Questions include education level and, where applicable, colleges attended and degrees earned (Common App guide).

routine.question: Are there circumstances or challenges that help explain your application?
routine.evidence: Michigan describes the Common App’s optional challenges-and-circumstances question; UC provides additional comments for unusual circumstances or clarification (Michigan, UC).

commonAppIntro: For 2026–27, the seven official options cover the following subjects; these are concise summaries rather than the full prompts (Common App official prompts).
commonAppChoices: Background, identity, interest, or talent: Share an essential part of your story (Common App).
Challenge, setback, or failure: Explain its effect on you and what you learned (Common App).
Questioning a belief or idea: Explain what prompted your thinking and the outcome (Common App).
Gratitude: Reflect on a surprising act of kindness and its influence on you (Common App).
Personal growth: Discuss an accomplishment, event, or realization that changed your understanding (Common App).
Intellectual curiosity: Describe a captivating topic and how you learn more about it (Common App).
Topic of your choice: Use an existing essay, another prompt, or a prompt of your own design (Common App).
commonAppClosing: These are alternatives, not seven essays to submit: the Common Application personal-essay instructions call for choosing one option, with a response between 250 and 650 words (Michigan’s published Common App instructions). Whether that personal essay is required depends on the college (Common App guide).

formats.name: UC
formats.format: Choose four of eight personal insight questions; each response has a 350-word maximum, and all question choices receive equal consideration (UC).

formats.name: Michigan
formats.format: Two university-specific essays are required for all applicants: a 100–300-word contribution essay and a 100–500-word school/curriculum-fit essay (Michigan).

formats.name: Yale
formats.format: For 2026–27, all first-year applicants identify academic areas and answer an academic-interest question of up to 200 words; Common App and Coalition applicants also answer three short takes of up to 200 characters each and choose one of three essays of up to 400 words (Yale).

formats.name: MIT
formats.format: For 2026–27, the page lists four main essays, approximately 100–200 words depending on the question, plus four short responses with room for 40–50 words each (MIT).

formats.name: Tufts
formats.format: Class of 2031 applicants answer two required short answers: a 75–150-word engagement question and a 100–200-word program-specific question (Tufts).

approachIntro: Build a bank of experiences before drafting polished answers. This is a suggested workflow, not an admissions requirement.

approach.title: Personal story
approach.text: Identify experiences that reveal your background, values, or identity.

approach.title: Academic interest
approach.text: List subjects, assignments, projects, books, or questions you have pursued.

approach.title: Challenge and growth
approach.text: Prepare an honest account of what happened, what you did, and what changed.

approach.title: Contribution and leadership
approach.text: Capture your role and impact in a group, workplace, family, or community.

approach.title: Meaningful commitment
approach.text: Identify an activity or responsibility that shows sustained effort.

approach.title: College fit
approach.text: Keep school-specific notes separate from reusable personal stories.

approachClosing: Use this list to brainstorm, then adapt to each actual prompt rather than reusing an answer unchanged. In particular, do not turn every additional-information box into another personal essay: UC explicitly says its additional-comments field should clarify relevant circumstances and should not be an essay (UC).
